preamble: Raising of the near-open front vowel [æ] to the close-mid front vowel [e]. It is best documented in the Old English dialects, where Anglian raised the long vowel ǣ to ē (West Saxon dǣd, Anglian dēd 'deed') and the Mercian 'Second Fronting' raised short æ to e (dæġ > deġ 'day'), and in Persian, where the word-final front vowel of Early New Persian was raised to [e] (xāna > xâne 'house').

examples.note: Post-brightening ǣ was raised to ē in Anglian but kept in West Saxon; also West Saxon slǣpan vs Anglian slēpan 'to sleep'.
Second Fronting, confined to part of the Mercian area, fronted /a/ to /æ/ and raised /æ/ to /e/; deġ is the Vespasian Psalter spelling.

examples.from: Classical Persian xāna /xaː.ˈna/ 'house' (final vowel fronted to [æ])
examples.note: Word-final /æ/ of Early New Persian mostly shifted to /e/ in contemporary Iranian Persian; Dari and Tajik keep final -a (xāna, xona).

sources: Wikipedia (2026). Phonological history of Old English. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonological_history_of_Old_English
